title: ‘An arm around the shoulder or a kick up the backside?’: Athlete perspectives on the expertise coaches require for the coach–athlete relationship in performance football
venue: International Journal of Sports Science & Coaching
abstract: The coach–athlete (C-A) relationship has been explored across multiple disciplines, with coaches’ ability to navigate these relationships widely regarded as central to coaching effectiveness. However, support for developing the expertise required by coaches to build effective C-A relationships remains underrepresented within formal coach education programmes. Increasingly, the C-A relationship is recognised as being shaped by broader socio-cultural contexts, highlighting the need to examine relational processes within the specific environments in which they occur. Significantly, this study foregrounds athletes’ perspectives from the highest levels of the professional game to explore how coaches’ relational expertise is perceived, interpreted, and experienced within C-A relationships. Semi-structured interviews were conducted with eight male and female professional athletes (n = 4 male, n = 4 female) competing in, or with significant experience of, high-performance football environments. Inductive reflexive thematic analysis generated four themes: (1) Beyond ‘building relationships’: towards a more considered position (2) The self as the cornerstone of relational practice; (3) Challenging dyadic conceptions of the C-A relationship; and (4) Developing relational astuteness: noticing, negotiating and influencing. The paper provides important contextually situated, athlete-centred insights into the expertise coaches require to develop effective C-A relationships.

title: ‘It's really complicated’. Analysis of Physical Education teachers’ difficulties in applying pedagogical models in the classroom
A feasibility and reliability pilot of a soccer-specific change-of-direction protocol incorporating ball possession, directional unpredictability, and limb dominance
abstract: Inroduction Laboratory-based change-of-direction (COD) assessments typically use predictable, ball-free tasks that inadequately reflect the perceptual and technical demands of soccer. This pilot study primarily assessed the feasibility of implementing a soccer-specific COD protocol incorporating ball possession, directional unpredictability, and limb dominance. Secondary objectives were to evaluate the intra- and inter-rater reliability of the Cutting Movement Assessment Score (CMAS) and to obtain exploratory estimates of variability in performance and biomechanical outcomes to inform the design and sample-size planning of a subsequent confirmatory trial. Methods Twenty-five trained male soccer players (Tier 2; age: 21.3 ± 1.9 years) completed eight COD conditions combining ball possession (with/without), directional predictability (predictable/unpredictable), and plant leg (dominant/non-dominant). Feasibility outcomes included recruitment, retention, valid-trial yield, session duration, and equipment performance. Reliability of the total CMAS score was assessed using two-way random-effects, absolute-agreement intraclass correlation coefficients (ICC₂,₁), while item-level agreement was assessed using Cohen’s κ . Preliminary outcomes included COD time, sprint-normalized COD deficit, CMAS score, peak vertical ground reaction force, peak braking force, and the horizontal-to-vertical braking force ratio. Results Recruitment efficiency was 52.1% (25 of 48 screened individuals), participant retention was 100%, and 92.7% of planned trials met the predefined validity criteria. title: Changes in motor performance associated with a four-week rope skipping intervention in primary school children: an exploratory quasi-experimental study using the DMT 6–18
venue: Frontiers in Sports and Active Living
abstract: Background Rope skipping is a scalable activity with demonstrated positive effects on children's motor coordination and physical fitness. However, little is known about its effects on overall motor performance as comprehensively assessed by the Deutscher Motorik-Test 6–18 (DMT), or which specific motor domains are most responsive to a short-term school-based rope skipping intervention. Objective This exploratory study examined changes in overall motor performance and specific motor abilities associated with a four-week Skipping Hearts rope skipping intervention in primary school children using the DMT 6–18. Methods In this quasi-experimental pretest–posttest study, 9- to 10-year-old primary school children ( n = 52; 21 intervention, 31 control) participated in either a four-week rope skipping intervention within regular physical education or continued with regular physical education (control group). Motor performance was assessed before and after the intervention using the DMT's eight standardized subtests and the DMT total score. Between-group differences in pre-post changes were analyzed using analysis of covariance (ANCOVA), complemented by class-level and sensitivity analyses. Reported p -values and CIs derive from individual-level analyses without adjustment for within-class dependence. Results Children in the intervention group demonstrated significantly greater improvements in overall motor performance than those in the control group [ F (1, 49) = 29.30, p < 0.001, partial η 2 = 0.35; adjusted mean difference = 6.92 standard-score points, 95% CI (4.35, 9.50)]. Excluding jumping sideways, which differed markedly at baseline, attenuated but did not eliminate this difference [5.86 points, 95% CI (3.00, 8.72)]. title: Prevalence of physical activity and perceived benefits and barriers among adults in the kingdom of Bahrain: an analytical cross-sectional study
venue: Frontiers in Sports and Active Living
abstract: Introduction Physical inactivity is a major modifiable risk factor for non-communicable diseases and premature mortality. However, evidence regarding physical activity levels and their determinants in Bahrain remains limited. This study aimed to assess physical activity prevalence among adults in Bahrain, explore perceived barriers and facilitators, and identify factors associated with physical activity participation. Methods An analytical cross-sectional study was conducted among adults residing in Bahrain using an online questionnaire distributed through snowball sampling. Physical activity was assessed using the International Physical Activity Questionnaire-Short Form (IPAQ-SF), with participants classified as physically active if they achieved ≥600 MET-minutes/week. Perceived benefits and barriers were assessed using an adapted Exercise Benefits/Barriers Scale. Sleep duration and perceived stress were evaluated using selected components of the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index and the Perceived Stress Scale (PSS-4), respectively. Data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, chi-square tests, and multivariable logistic regression. Results Of 383 participants, 365 provided complete physical activity data. Overall, 53.4% (95% CI: 48.3-58.5%) were physically active, while 46.6% were physically inactive. Walking was the most common activity, whereas vigorous-intensity activity was infrequent. Mean sedentary time was 6.8 hours/day. The most frequently reported barriers were adverse weather conditions (61.6%) and work or household time constraints (53.3%). In adjusted analyses, women had significantly lower odds of being physically active than men (adjusted OR: 0.309, 95% CI: 0.150–0.637; p = 0.001). title: Exploring the degeneracy and creativity of passing behaviors from discrete passing variables in small-sided soccer games
abstract: The aim of this study was to explore the degeneracy and creativity of passing behaviors hidden behind the number of passes in small-sided games to inform football coaches’ training programmes. Based on ecological dynamics, the constraint of pitch size was manipulated to incorporate passing numbers, penetrative passing behaviours and creative passing behaviours together in small-sided games. Twenty U-19 male football players played 10 small-sided games on two different sizes of pitches. The results found that the number of passes (p = . 433, Cohen’s d = 0.39, small effect size) and passing fluency (p = .645, Cohen’s d = 0.22, small effect size) did not differ significantly between the two different sizes of pitches; whereas in Pitch 1 (35 m × 20 m), there was more penetrative passing behaviours (p = . 052, Cohen’s d = 1.22, large effect); in Pitch 2 (25 m × 15 m), players emerged with greater versatility in passing behaviours (p = .028, Cohen’s d = 1.50, large effect) and passing attempts (p = .170, Cohen’s d = 0.75, medium effect); and there were two more original passing actions emerging from Pitch 2 than from Pitch 1. This suggest that coaches cannot rely solely on the number of passes to develop players’ passing behaviour in small-sided games.Coaches should deeply understand the eco-dynamic value of passing behaviours, and be skilled at exploring the degeneracy,variability and creativity of passing behaviours in order to develop more scientific training plans and enhance the creativity of soccer players.

title: Hydroclimatic evolution under changing westerly–monsoon influences in northeastern China since the Late Glacial
abstract: Hydroclimatic variability in the transition zone between the East Asian summer monsoon and mid-latitude westerlies reflects the combined influence of these two circulation systems. Understanding how their relative influences have changed over time is essential for interpreting long-term regional moisture variability. Here, we reconstructed regional hydroclimatic changes since 14.3 ka BP using a continuous lacustrine sequence from Aranji Nur, a closed lake on the southwestern margin of the Hulunbuir Grassland in northeastern China. Sediment grain-size distributions were analyzed and compared with regional paleoclimate and environmental records. Four major hydroclimatic stages were identified: relatively dry conditions during 14.3–9.2 ka BP, increased effective moisture during 9.2–4.8 ka BP, gradually declining moisture during 4.8–1.5 ka BP, and renewed aridification since 1.5 ka BP. Variations in sediment grain size, particularly sand content, were broadly consistent with changes in regional moisture availability and surface stability, reflecting the combined effects of vegetation cover, sediment availability, aeolian transport, and local depositional processes. Comparison with regional records suggests that increased moisture availability during the early to middle Holocene was associated with stronger monsoonal influence and potentially additional moisture supplied by the westerlies. Subsequent drying coincided with weakening monsoonal influence and changes in the position of the westerly jet that may have reduced effective moisture transport to the study region. These findings highlight the importance of both circulation intensity and spatial changes in atmospheric circulation and associated moisture transport pathways in shaping long-term hydroclimatic evolution acro

title: Acute Neuromuscular and Performance Adaptations to PAPE—Focused Warm-Up Strategies in Rowing
abstract: Post-activation performance enhancement (PAPE) warm-up practices have received considerable interest due to their potential to acutely enhance neuromuscular output and athletic performance. In this regard, flywheel-based warm-ups have gained recognition as an innovative and effective strategy, particularly relevant in high-intensity sports such as rowing, where explosive power and neuromuscular coordination are key determinants of performance. Through a randomized crossover design, we investigated the acute effects of flywheel-based and general warm-up protocols on neuromuscular performance and 500-m rowing ergometer output in 32 male rowers (16 collegiate and 16 recreational). Post-warm-up assessments included grip strength, the countermovement jump, the isometric mid-thigh pull, the dynamic strength index and 500-m time trials. Collegiate rowers significantly improved 500-m rowing time (diff: 4.06%; p = 0.02, d = 0.84) and the dynamic strength index (diff: 28.44%; p = 0.01, d = −0.98) following the flywheel protocol, despite reductions in isometric mid-thigh pull force (diff: −17.78%; p = 0.03, d = 0.80). Recreational rowers, in contrast, experienced greater strength decline and no performance gains (diff: 1.92%; p = 0.35; d = 0.36). Across all participants, the dynamic strength index increased post-warm-up, indicating enhanced neuromuscular efficiency. These results suggest that flywheel warm-ups can elicit post-activation performance enhancement in trained athletes, while general warm-ups may be more appropriate for less trained individuals. The findings underscore the importance of tailoring warm-up strategies to the athlete’s training status to optimize performance outcomes in rowing and other power-endurance sports.

title: Suicide prevention capacity in Kalaallit Nunaat (Greenland) through local gatekeeper training: a qualitative evaluation of the Lifeline Course programme.
abstract: Suicide prevention in Kalaallit Nunaat (Greenland) unfolds within small communities where Kalaallit Inuit frontline workers often carry both professional responsibilities for supporting individuals at risk of suicide and personal experiences of suicide among family members, friends, or community members. Frontline workers include both formally trained professionals (e.g. teachers, nurses, and social workers) and community-based workers whose helping roles are grounded in lived experience, local knowledge, and community responsibility. Although certified gatekeeper training programmes are widely used internationally, little is known about their long-term relevance in Indigenous Arctic contexts. This study explores how Kalaallit Inuit frontline workers experienced the Lifeline Course, a certified gatekeeper training programme adapted for Kalaallit Nunaat, three years after completion. Seven Kalaallit Inuit frontline workers from two municipalities participated in semi-structured interviews conducted in Kalaallisut. Participants described sustained increases in confidence and reduced fear when supporting people at risk of suicide. The training's structured approach and culturally resonant communication tools facilitated direct and sincere conversations in Kalaallisut. Participants also highlighted the emotional complexity of working in communities affected by suicide and described suicide prevention as a shared community responsibility strengthened through collaboration and mutual support. Findings suggest that the long-term value of gatekeeper training depends not only on skill acquisition but also on strengthening the cultural, relational, and emotional foundations that support suicide-prevention work.

title: Foot pressure dynamics during Taijiquan standing meditation.
abstract: Taijiquan is a low-impact mind-body training practice integrating mindfulness, balance, and controlled movement. Among its foundational practices, standing meditation (Zhan Zhuang) serves as a precursor to dynamic forms, fostering balance, relaxation, and internal focus. While Taijiquan's benefits are well-documented, limited quantitative research has explored the foot pressure dynamics underpinning skill acquisition, particularly during standing meditation. This exploratory pilot study investigated whether frequency-domain plantar-force features could provide preliminary quantitative indicators associated with practitioner skill progression across beginner, intermediate, and advanced competency levels. A pressure mat was used to analyze regional foot pressures variations in the time and frequency domain. Twenty-three participants, categorized into beginner, intermediate, and advanced levels, performed controlled standing stances under standardized conditions. The data were analyzed using conventional unsupervised cluster algorithms (k-means, hierarchical, DBSCAN), and an established statistical hypothesis-testing framework. Advanced practitioners demonstrated distinct low-frequency oscillatory patterns compared with beginners. Unsupervised clustering revealed preliminary group structure consistent with practitioner experience without using expert-defined labels.
